TCS cut 12,000+ jobs in an AI-driven overhaul last year. It just posted its best hiring quarter in 12 months.

The cuts came in July 2025, about 2% of the workforce, concentrated in middle and senior management, the layer TCS called part of a "future-ready transformation" for AI-first delivery.

Headcount fell for three straight quarters after that.

Then, in results announced July 9 this year, TCS added 9,279 people net, roughly 14,000 of them fresh graduates straight off campus, its strongest hiring quarter in a year. Attrition held flat at 13.6% through the quarter, so this wasn't fewer people quitting. It was a deliberate call to add headcount right as TCS announced it had won "multiple AI transformation deals."

Same company. Same restructuring story. Two opposite-looking headlines, twelve months apart.

Put together, the real pattern isn't "AI is taking Indian IT jobs." It's that AI is re-sorting them fast, inside the same company, inside the same year (which is why either number, read alone, tells you almost nothing).

The useful question isn't whether AI is coming for your role. It's whether your current project reads, on paper, as AI-delivery work or as the layer getting compressed.

Title: Kill It or Keep It: The Five-Question Test That Decides What AI Should Do in Your Job

At some point this year, probably on an ordinary Tuesday, you looked at a task on your desk and wondered whether you should still be doing it by hand.

Maybe it was the monthly compliance report built from three spreadsheets. Maybe it was the fourth file noting of the day, or the OPD (Outpatient Department) roster, or the minutes of a meeting that ended an hour ago and is already fading.

You know AI could probably help. What you don't have is a way to decide. Not a vague feeling. A procedure.

That is what this post gives you. We call it the Kill It or Keep It test: five questions you ask about any recurring task, and four honest verdicts that come out the other side. It takes about three minutes per task. By the end of this post you will have run it on your own work.

Why you never got a decision procedure

Almost everything written about AI and jobs comes in two flavours.

The first is hype: AI will do everything, adapt or perish. The second is reassurance: AI can never replace human judgment, relax. Both are useless on a Tuesday afternoon, because both talk about your job. Jobs are the wrong unit of analysis.

Jobs do not get automated. Tasks do. Your job is a bundle of forty tasks, and AI's usefulness varies wildly across the bundle. The officer who dismisses AI because "it cannot understand governance" is right about six of his tasks and wrong about twenty. The manager who fears AI will replace her is afraid of something that will actually just eat her most boring Thursday hours.

So the first move is to stop asking "is my job safe" and start asking "which of my tasks should move." That question has an answer you can compute.

The five questions

Take one recurring task. Ask these five questions about it.

1. How often do you do it?
Weekly or more, score it high. Below monthly, score it low. Automation has a setup cost: learning the prompt, building the habit, checking the output until you trust it. A task you do twice a year rarely pays that back. The compliance report you build every single week pays it back forty times over.

2. Do the inputs arrive in a knowable shape?
Some tasks feed on structured material: documents, forms, precedents, data files, last month's version. Others feed on ambient context that lives in your head, in corridor conversations, in fifteen years of knowing how your department works. AI is excellent with the first kind and blind to the second. A grievance reply built from the complaint letter and your standard positions is structured. Reading the room in a tense review meeting is not.

3. Can you verify the output faster than you could produce it?
This is the most underrated question in the entire test, so slow down here. The best AI handoffs live inside an asymmetry: producing the draft takes you two hours, checking a draft takes you ten minutes. Wherever that gap is wide, AI fits. Wherever checking is as slow as doing, be careful. If you cannot judge whether the output is right without redoing the work, you have not saved time. You have added a review layer to a task you still effectively do.

4. What breaks if the output is wrong?
Be honest about the blast radius. A clumsy internal summary costs a little embarrassment. A wrong figure in an audit response, a misstated clause in a legal filing, a dosage error in a clinical document: these cost careers and worse. High stakes does not disqualify a task. It changes the verdict from "hand it over" to "hand over the effort, keep the checking."

5. Must a human own it?
Some tasks carry accountability that cannot move, no matter what the technology does. A government officer's signature on a file noting is statutory. A doctor's discharge decision is clinical responsibility. A manager's appraisal of a person is a commitment made by a person. For these, the question is never whether AI replaces you. It is how much of the surrounding effort AI can absorb while the ownership stays exactly where it is.

The four verdicts

The test's name says kill or keep, but honest scoring produces four buckets, not two.

KILL: high frequency, structured inputs, quick to verify, low stakes. Meeting minutes. Status summaries. Reformatting. First drafts of routine correspondence. Hand these over completely and stop thinking about them. This is not laziness. It is the correct allocation of a scarce resource, which is you.

SHRINK: structured and verifiable, but the stakes are real. Audit preparation. RTI (Right to Information) draft responses. Grievance replies. Budget notes. AI produces the 80 percent draft, you verify line by line and sign. The typing goes. The signature stays. For most professionals in government, healthcare and finance, this is the biggest bucket, and it is where the wage premium for AI skills actually lives.

SPLIT: the task is really two tasks wearing one name. A board deck is (a) deciding what to argue and (b) producing slides. File noting is (a) judgment about the case and (b) drafting prose in the prescribed format. Splitting means you notice the seam, kill the (b), and keep the (a). Most resistance that sounds like "AI cannot do my job" dissolves here, because the part AI cannot do was never the part that ate your hours.

KEEP: the value is the human. Negotiation. A difficult conversation with a patient's family. Building trust with a new stakeholder. Mentoring. Anything where the deliverable is the relationship. Keep these without guilt, and notice something important: the hours the other three buckets free up should flow here, because this is the work that compounds your career.

The three traps

Run the test naively and you will fall into one of three holes. Watch for them.

Trap one: killing a load-bearing task. Sometimes the memo was never the deliverable. Writing the memo was how you came to understand the problem, and the understanding is what your boss actually pays for. Before killing anything, ask: what do I learn by doing this manually, and where else will I learn it? If there is no other place, the task is load-bearing. Shrink it instead of killing it, and stay close.

Trap two: keeping out of identity. People protect the tasks they are best at, because being the person who writes the cleanest notes or builds the tightest decks is who they are at the office. If a task scores kill on all five questions and you still refuse, the reason is not in the workflow. It is in the mirror. That is a real thing to work through. It is not a scoring error.

Trap three: automating a process that should not exist. If the weekly report exists because someone asked for it in 2019 and nobody ever cancelled it, the verdict is not "kill it with AI." The verdict is kill it, full stop. Automating a pointless process makes it permanent. The test is also an audit of your workload, and some tasks fail the audit entirely.

Run it this week

Here is the exercise we give in the first week of our bootcamp, and it works on paper as well as it works in a classroom.

List your ten most recurring tasks. Real ones, from your actual week, in your actual words: "prepare the Monday review file," not "stakeholder communication." Run each through the five questions. Write a one-letter verdict next to each: K (kill), S (shrink), P (split), KP (keep).

Most professionals who do this honestly find two tasks to kill, four to shrink, two to split, and two to keep. That is roughly ten hours a week sitting in the first three buckets. The professionals earning the 56 percent AI wage premium are not smarter than you. They ran some version of this test, and then they acted on the verdicts.

The follow-up question that separates the two groups: when the hours come back, where do they go? If freed time just absorbs into more email, the test changed nothing. Decide in advance which KEEP task gets the reclaimed hours.

If you want company while you do it, the Garage Labs community is full of professionals running exactly this exercise on file notings, hospital rosters and audit files. Join at garagelabstech.com/community. And if you want to go from verdicts to actually building the AI workflows that execute them, Cohort 50 of our AI Accelerator Bootcamp starts August 1st: ten weeks, live and mentor-led, no tech background needed, twenty seats.

Kill the typing. Keep the judgment. That is the whole trick.

TITLE: Engagement Proposal — Prove Unit Economics Before You Scale the Build

OPENING: The thing that keeps most founders up at night isn't whether the technology will work. It's spending six months and real money on a full build, then discovering on day 181 that the business model doesn't hold. You're evaluating build partners right now, and most of them will pitch you the whole vision and a lot of hours up front. We want to do the opposite.

Before we build anything for scale, we prove that families will pay for it. That one decision changes how everything else gets built. We start with a short commercial validation sprint (we call it P0) that answers the only question a spreadsheet can't: will real families go through the journey and hand over ₹65,000? Once we know that, and know it with real data, the full build gets engineered around what actually works instead of what we guessed would work.

SECTION 4 (the sprint): "Before we build for scale, we prove someone will pay for it. That changes everything about how we build." TrueArq already has a working Scout AI agent and a waitlist. This sprint doesn't test whether voice AI works; you've already shown that it does. It tests three things a spreadsheet can't tell you: whether families finish the whole journey, what it actually costs to acquire and serve one of them, and whether they'll pay ₹65,000 for Immersive at the real price. To find that out fast, we keep P0 deliberately thin: a light wrapper around what already exists, with a human coach standing in for anything we'd otherwise have to build.

SECTION 3 (smarter build): Once P0 tells us families will pay, the real build starts, and it starts smarter. After we've watched fifty families go through the journey, we know where the automation actually needs to go. Maybe the bottleneck isn't the voice agent. Maybe it's the human handoff, or a feature families kept asking for that nobody had scoped. That's not a smaller build. It's a build aimed at what works instead of what we assumed.

CLOSING: The risk of a six-month build is that you find out the business model doesn't work on day 181, with the money already spent. The risk of a two-week sprint is that you spend a little and learn you need to adjust. Only one of those is recoverable. That's the whole reason to start here.

# Accessibility Audit — Product Brief & Working Doc (v0.3)

## 1. TL;DR
An honest, anti-overlay accessibility auditor for websites. Free instant URL scan → risk-scored WCAG/508 report → paid human-assisted remediation → recurring monitoring. We sell risk reduction, remediation, and ongoing drift detection, not a fake "one-click compliance" widget. Fast to launch because it reuses the Answer Ready audit engine (an existing shipped URL-scan → score → report product), and it lands on a real, fear-driven, SMB-heavy market with structural willingness-to-pay.
One-liner: "Honest accessibility risk audit. No overlay gimmicks. No lawsuit-proof claims."
Spec decision: lead with SMB ecommerce for fast validation, use the founder's Optum/Section-508 background as a trust signal and premium enterprise lane, monetize first through audit/DFY cashflow, build true MRR through monitoring subscriptions.

## 2. Market validation (US)
- Federal web-accessibility lawsuits 2025: 3,117 (+27% YoY). Total incl. NY/CA state courts: 5,000+.
- Demand letters sent 2025 (the real funnel): ~35,000–50,000.
- 64% of sued firms under $25M revenue; ecommerce/retail ≈ 70% of suits.
- Typical demand-letter settlement $5,000–$25,000; legal defense if fought $30,000–$175,000.
Read: large, growing, fear-driven, SMB-heavy; willingness-to-pay is structural.

## 3. The wedge — anti-overlay, "honest audit"
Incumbents imploding: accessiBe $1M FTC penalty (2025) for falsely claiming AI makes sites WCAG-compliant; 25% of ADA suits now cite overlays as barriers; class actions against accessiBe and UserWay by SMBs who bought the overlay and got sued anyway; disability community actively rejects overlays. Overlay pricing: $49–199/mo/site; AudioEye $199+/mo.
Positioning effectively endorsed by the FTC: honest audit + real remediation, explicitly not an overlay and not a compliance guarantee.

## 4. Unfair advantages
1. Founder's Section 508 experience at Optum (enterprise healthcare remediation) — domain credibility + premium 508/public-sector/healthcare lane.
2. Answer Ready engine ~70% reusable (scorer framework, report viewer, rate-limits, SSRF guard).
3. AI-infra skill: cheap fast detection + plain-English explanations.
4. Free real-scan moat: landing page runs a real instant WCAG scan from day one; prospects self-qualify.

## 5. Product definition
Offer ladder: Free hook (URL scan → risk score, top violations, screenshots) → Audit $199 (market: $1,250–2,750 for full manual audits) → DFY remediation $499–1,500+ (market $250–550/page) → Monitoring/Managed $49–199/mo per site (re-scans, regression alerts, refreshed accessibility statement).
Division of labor: AI does detection/explanation/prioritization/report; humans do code-level remediation. Automated scans catch only ~30–40% of WCAG issues, which is exactly why overlays fail; the human tier is the honest necessity and the margin.
DFY scope honesty: quotes carry explicit exclusions and a "cannot remediate" path (platform-locked code like Shopify checkout internals).
Scan surface: free scan covers publicly reachable pages only; paid detailed audit covers authenticated flows (checkout, account, gated forms) via client-granted access — a second honest upsell axis alongside the 30/70 mechanic.
$5k MRR math: DFY is one-time cash, not MRR. Monitoring is the MRR engine (~50 sites × $99/mo). DFY sales fund early months and auto-convert into monitoring subscriptions because sites drift out of compliance.

## 6. Positioning & messaging
Core promise: "Honest accessibility risk audit. No overlay gimmicks. No lawsuit-proof claims."
Contrast hooks: "That accessibility widget isn't protecting you — it's a lawsuit waiting to happen." / "Is your overlay actually compliant? Scan and find out (free)."
Trust signals: real WCAG findings, screenshots, severity, founder's 508 credentials, transparent methodology.
Never say: guaranteed compliant, lawsuit-proof, one-click, AI-fixes-automatically.
SMB copy uses ADA/WCAG only; "508" reserved for the enterprise/public-sector lane.

## 6A. Competitive landscape
Overlays (accessiBe, UserWay, EqualWeb): cheap, credibility-damaged. Hybrid platforms (AudioEye, Level Access, Silktide): credible, expensive/complex for SMBs. Automated checkers (WAVE, axe, Lighthouse): trusted but buyer must interpret and fix. Consultancies (Deque, TPGi): high credibility, slow, no instant funnel. Legal firms: reactive, expensive. Agencies: can fix, weak audit product.
Read: the gap is "instant enough to convert, honest enough to trust, practical enough to fix."

## 6B. USP
"The honest accessibility audit for SMB websites: instant WCAG risk scan, human-prioritized remediation plan, and done-for-you fixes without overlay gimmicks or false compliance guarantees."
Differentiators: anti-overlay trust position; instant scan + human pathway; business-risk translation (user impact, conversion risk, demand-letter exposure, fix effort); existing audit engine; founder 508/Optum credibility; DFY-first monetization ($5k/mo doesn't need SaaS scale).
Positioning formula: For SMB ecommerce owners and agencies who worry their site is inaccessible or exposed to ADA demand letters, our product provides an honest WCAG risk audit and remediation path. Unlike overlays that claim one-click compliance or raw scanners that dump issues, we show concrete evidence, prioritize business risk, and can fix the underlying site.

## 7. ICP
Primary: SMB ecommerce on Shopify/WooCommerce/Webflow/WordPress (70% of suits, visible failures, easy to find). Agencies as reseller channel. Secondary/premium: Section 508 public-sector vendors, gov contractors, healthcare (bigger deals, longer cycles) — a credibility CTA from day one, not the validation focus.

## 8. GTM / distribution
Audit-as-lead-magnet (free scan IS the funnel); SEO on high-intent queries ("ADA compliance checker", "accessiBe alternative"); anti-overlay content riding the overlay-lawsuit news cycle; agency partnerships (resell audits + DFY); build-in-public ("I scanned 100 SMB sites — here's what's about to get them sued").

## 9. Legal guardrail (the single most important constraint)
Never claim guaranteed compliance / lawsuit-proof / one-click. Frame as AI-assisted WCAG risk audit + prioritized remediation toward conformance. Reports private to requester (no site-shaming). Honest scoring: v1 score is a severity-weighted count of machine-detected violations, labeled "scan severity", never "lawsuit risk"; every AI output rule-backed + human-reviewed.

## 10. 14-day validation plan (sell-before-build)
Pre-outreach gates: third-party scanning policy; fulfillment owner named.
Landing page with real free scan (scan-failure fallback converts failures to leads; our own site and reports must pass WCAG 2.1 AA, results published). Manual/semi-automated audits for 10–20 target sites. Outreach to agencies + store owners. Sell 3 paid remediation packages before building automation.
Outreach script: lead with a concrete mini-finding ("keyboard users can't complete checkout"), never lawsuits/ADA in first touch; real identity; one follow-up max.
Offer for validation: free mini-scan → $199–499 express audit ("express review", not "audit" — professionals check) → $750–2,500+ DFY.
Metrics: minimum success = 3 paid audits or 1 DFY from 100+ qualified prospects (days 14–21 allowed for closes); monitoring intent measured (≥1 paid commitment or 3 documented "I'd pay $X/mo"); funnel tracked scans→leads→replies→calls→paid with day-5/10 checkpoints; capture whether agencies or direct owners convert faster and which platform converts best.

## 12. Key open dependencies
Who fulfills DFY (founder/contractor/agency); lightweight legal review of disclaimers before first sale; India-based founder selling US legal-risk service (entity, E&O insurance, MSA) settled before first paid sale; will SMBs pay monthly to STAY audited or treat compliance as one-and-done?

## Known caveats (self-recorded)
The "moat" is a speed + credibility head start, not structural defensibility; durable assets are reputation and the monitoring base. DFY delivery economics unmodeled (first 3 jobs double as cost-model exercise). Market-data sources partly vendor-published. The ~70% engine-reuse figure is an assumption to verify.

CORE THESIS: Nebius is a Gartner-recognized Visionary in Cloud AI Infrastructure (2026 MQ), not yet a Leader, and that gap is honest and explainable: it's about reference density, geographic scope, and use-case breadth, not technical quality. Nebius's actual technical strength (training reliability, co-engineering depth, cost) is real and independently corroborated (SemiAnalysis ClusterMAX Gold tier, MLPerf-verified results), but Nebius has zero named M&E customers in inference (Token Factory's public customers are Brave, Revolut, Sword Health, all outside M&E) and its flagship training-side proof (Higgsfield, Recraft, Black Forest Labs) is concentrated in one demand cluster: training-scale multimodal generation.

STRUCTURE: (1) Nebius's own platform first (training infra, Token Factory, Eigen AI acquisition-in-progress, compliance), stated precisely with independent sources, including real scrutiny (SemiAnalysis's own critique of Nebius's MTBF framing as "cherry-picked," and analyst skepticism on Meta/Microsoft customer concentration and depreciation accounting). (2) Gartner Visionary positioning: why AWS/Google/Azure/Alibaba/Huawei/Oracle are Leaders and Nebius/CoreWeave/Crusoe are Visionaries, using Gartner's actual evaluation criteria, with evidence that even CoreWeave (elite technical benchmarks, 9/10 top labs, Platinum ClusterMAX) is still only a Visionary, supporting "execution gap tracks scale not tech quality." (3) Four infrastructure demand clusters, each with 2-3 named companies and honest current-state framing: training-scale multimodal generation (Higgsfield, Recraft, Black Forest Labs, fal.ai as serving-layer context; strongest Nebius proof) / real-time inference (ElevenLabs, Twelve Labs; zero named Nebius M&E proof, a real gap stated plainly) / proprietary training for studios (Lionsgate+Runway as the real Western-studio precedent; ByteDance explicitly rejected as an example because Disney/Paramount/WB/Sony/Netflix are actively litigating against ByteDance's Seedance over IP infringement, and TikTok was forced into forced divestiture over CCP data-access concerns, the opposite of what Nebius's sovereignty pitch needs) / edge and embedded inference (World Labs, General Intuition; General Intuition explicitly chose CoreWeave for its next compute scale-up, a named competitive loss, stated honestly not hidden). (4) Competitive wedge: against CoreWeave, contest financial durability and customer concentration, not benchmarks (CoreWeave has GAAP net loss $740M and 1% adjusted operating margin despite $2.1B Q1 revenue); against Crusoe, the distinction is categorical (Crusoe is a vertically-integrated power-plus-compute utility selling to hyperscalers, not a peer AI-native cloud); against Leaders, don't fight on breadth, own the wedge of specialization plus structural neutrality (no owned media/content business, unlike AWS/MGM/Project NARA or Google/Veo/Imagen hosted against its own customers). (5) A practical layer: discovery questions to sort a prospect into the right demand cluster, and objection handling for "you're smaller/newer," "Gartner has you below AWS," "no studio reference yet," "Eigen AI is still integrating."

CENTRAL QUESTION THE REPORT ANSWERS: why would a Runway or a similar company choose Nebius over AWS for training or inference. ANSWER: because Nebius is built for and willing to specialize in the specific constraints of M&E generative workloads (training reliability at scale, co-engineering depth, cost transparency) and carries no structural conflict of interest, while the Leaders have broader reference bases and execution scale but also real, evidenced content-business conflicts of interest.
